metadata.title: Measuring education: Do we need a plethora of assessment studies or just a single score?
metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study conducts country-level correlational comparisons using published ILSA country mean scores (e.g., TIMSS 2019, PISA 2000–2018, ICCS 2016, ICILS 2018) rather than student-level microdata. Because the analysis is based on aggregated country means, the paper does not describe the application of complex survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife). The methodology therefore does not provide a weight variable name or replicate design details, and weighting is not operationalized in the reported analyses. The main preprocessing described is robustness replication for an OECD-only subset and the use of multidimensional scaling to visualize cross-assessment similarity.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this paper are country mean achievement scores and their cross-assessment correlations (and derived distance/correlation structures for multidimensional scaling), not student-level cognitive outcomes with plausible values. As a result, plausible-value generation/combination procedures are not applicable to the reported analysis. Missing-data handling is not reported because the paper does not perform student-level imputation or PV-based estimation; instead, it discusses practical constraints and inclusion of countries/regions that may not fully meet sampling criteria, which affects validity/reliability rather than being handled via statistical missing-data procedures.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used all countries participating in the selected ILSA cycles/domains for the correlational and multidimensional scaling analyses, with robustness replication using a subset of OECD countries. The paper notes that some countries/regions may not have met sampling criteria (or nearly met them after school replacement) and that these were included to build a more comprehensive picture; no student-level inclusion/exclusion rules are specified.

data.outcome_summary: This paper is not an empirical ML prediction study; it examines how different ILSAs relate by computing correlations between country mean scores across domains (mathematics, science, reading, civic education, computer and information literacy, and other PISA/TIMSS add-ons) and by visualizing similarity using multidimensional scaling. It reports a very high correlation between TIMSS 2019 mathematics and science country means (r = 0.94) for both Grade 4 and Grade 8, suggesting limited added value of a separate science score when a math score is already available. In contrast, correlations between TIMSS 2019 mathematics and ICCS 2016 (Grade 8) are described as driven by outliers, with some countries showing large discrepancies (e.g., Latvia vs Norway). The paper also finds that the hypothesized pattern of higher correlations for assessments closer in time is not supported for PISA reading (2000–2018), and it highlights PISA linking errors up to 2012 as a limitation. Overall, it argues that non-core domains (ICCS/ICILS) can change country interpretations beyond core domains (math/science/reading), informing policy decisions about which assessments to prioritize.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper is a correlational/cross-assessment comparability study using country-level mean scores and multidimensional scaling, not a student-level predictive modeling analysis. Consequently, there is no ML algorithm training/evaluation, no plausible-value estimation pipeline, and no student-level analytic sample size to extract. The absence of per-country student counts and PV/missing-data procedures is consistent with the study’s design (aggregated country means rather than microdata).
